Hi:

If your data are nested, then the facet_grid() plot is correct, because nesting, by definition, means that the levels of the second factor are uniquely associated with a specific level of the first. Unfortunately, faceting, either in ggplot2 or lattice, does not support nesting natively.

It's not too hard to envision what you might want: a faceted plot something of the form

                   TTTY6B                                              TTYH1
 |      NM_A       |        NM_B      ||         NM_C    |     NM_D    |     NM_E   

(or an analogous stacked version)

but neither ggplot2 nor lattice is capable of giving you such a structure. The best you can hope for is your initial facet_grid() graphic, which clearly illustrates the nested structure. If you want something closer to the outline above, you have to be a little more creative; i.e., you need to create separate plots for each gene and them paste them together using (some variant of) the grid package. Here's one approach:

# Create separate data frames for each gene,
# redefining the transcript factor so that it
# contains only the levels within a data frame

DF1 <- subset(DF, gene == "TTTY6B")
DF1$transcript <- factor(DF1$transcript)

DF2 <- subset(DF, gene == "TTYH1")
DF2$transcript <- factor(DF2$transcript)



# Create two potential versions of a 'nested' factor plot:

###########################
# Vertical version:

p1 <- ggplot(DF1, aes(x = time, y = tpm, color = treatment)) +
        geom_point(size = 3) +
        geom_smooth(se = FALSE, size = 1) + 
        facet_wrap(~ transcript, nrow = 1)
p2 <- p1 %+% DF2

p1 <- p1 + theme(legend.position = c(0.8, 0.8),
                 plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold")) +
      labs(x = NULL, title = "TTTY6B")

p2 <- p2 + theme(legend.position = "none",
                 plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold")) +
       ggtitle("TTYH1")

library(gridExtra)
grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 1)

##########################

# Horizontal version:

p3 <- ggplot(DF1, aes(x = time, y = tpm, color = treatment)) +
        geom_point(size = 3) +
        geom_smooth(se = FALSE, size = 1) + 
        facet_wrap(~ transcript, nrow = 1)
p4 <- p3 %+% DF2

p3 <- p3 + theme(legend.position = c(0.8, 0.9),
                 plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
                 panel.margin = unit(0.1, "in")) +
           ggtitle("TTTY6B") + ylab(NULL)

p4 <- p4 + theme(legend.position = "none",
                 plot.title = element_text(size = 13, face = "bold"),
                 panel.margin = unit(0.1, "in")) +
           ggtitle("TTYH1")


library(grid)

# Function to position graphical objects
vplayout <- function(x, y)
    viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)

# Create a new page and place the graphical objects
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(1, 10)))

print(p4, vp = vplayout(1, 1:6))
print(p3, vp = vplayout(1, 7:10))


Feel free to tinker with it. Tip: If you're going to modify a ggplot, start from the top (by which I mean refresh the original graphical objects and then modify them). It will save you some headaches.

If you're happy with this, post it as a solution on the ggplot2 list.

Dennis

On Feb 15, 2013, at 2:37 PM, Dennis wrote:

Hi:

This is an exercise in 'understanding your data structure'. At present, gene is utterly unnecessary because you have it included among the levels of transcript. If you took gene out (as an aesthetic) of the facet_wrap()ped graph, it would look exactly the same. As you have it constructed, transcript *appears* to be nested within gene, which is why the facet_grid() graphic has the pattern of missing panels that it has.

I don't know enough about gene expression data to fix this for you, but the critical question is whether transcript is intended to be nested within gene or crossed with it; in the latter case, the levels of transcript should be qualitatively 'independent' of those of gene - i.e, {1, 2, 3}. If gene and transcript are meant to be crossed, then you need to change the levels of transcript accordingly. 

I would have attempted to show you how one could do this, but an attempt to copy and paste your data into R failed because it all ran together:

+ genetranscripttreatmenttimetpm
+ oneoneFirstdrug03
+ oneoneFirstdrug14
...

If you're going to post data to an R-related list, please use dput() on the data object and copy/paste that instead. For example,

> DF <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = rpois(3, 2))
> dput(DF)
structure(list(x = 1:3, y = c(1, 2, 1)), .Names = c("x", "y"), row.names = c(NA, 
-3L), class = "data.frame")

Copy and paste the part that starts with structure(). The output of dput() precisely replicates the structure of your R object in text form. A potential helper can be confident that, by copy/pasting the output of dput() into her R session, the structure of the sent object is preserved. One cannot be so confident with data copied from who-knows-where into an e-mail, as you can see from the above.

Dennis
